15.title: Hanuman's whole personality
15.hook: a mountain carried across the sky, because one herb was needed
15.howItsDone: Seva is part of ordinary Hindu life: volunteers clean temples, cook and serve meals at festivals, and care for family and neighbors, and devotees look to Hanuman as the picture of selfless service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, arti. Your line was light passed hand to hand. At sunset, did the light go to anyone? Week three starts now, and it opens with words you do with your hands. Day fifteen.

Night, on a battlefield in Lanka. Lakshmana, Rama's brother, lies wounded, barely breathing. A healer says there is a cure: certain herbs that grow on a mountain far to the north, and they have to be here fast. Hanuman goes. He crosses the sky, finds the mountain, and then he stops. The herbs are hiding from him, the story says, and he can't tell which ones are needed. There's no time to go back and ask. So he solves it another way. He lifts the whole peak out of the ground and carries it back through the air, herbs and all. Lakshmana breathes. Hanuman has a monkey's face, the strength of the wind, and a picture of him hangs in homes and shops. Today's word is why.
screen: `A BROTHER WOUNDED. NO TIME TO LOSE.` → `HE CAN'T TELL WHICH HERB.` → `SO HE BRINGS THE MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Seva. Service. Not service as a job title, and not help with a receipt attached. Seva is doing what's needed because it's needed, with the self stepped out of the way. Hanuman is the tradition's living picture of it. Notice what the mountain story leaves out. There's no speech. No moment where he explains how hard it was. The whole story points at one thing: a man on the ground starts breathing again. The strength is enormous, and it's all aimed outward. The Ramayana does this with him more than once. When he leaps the ocean and finds Sita in Lanka, what he finally puts in Rama's hand is hers, not his: her jewel, and her message. Later devotional stories push the picture even further; people tell of him opening his own chest to show that Rama and Sita live inside it. Whatever he has, it's for someone else. And seva doesn't need a mountain. In temples and homes it's very ordinary work. Washing the floor before the festival. Chopping vegetables for a meal that strangers will eat. Sitting with a sick neighbor so the family can sleep. Nobody hands out credit for it, and that's part of the point. There's something else folded into the word. Some who practice it say seva done quietly works on the one doing it too: for as long as the hands are busy with someone else's need, the head gets a rest from itself. Hanuman's gifts were huge. The practice works with whatever size yours are.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your herb. Sit and breathe. Bring one thing to mind that you're good at. Cooking. Listening. Fixing a bike. Staying calm in a mess. Now let one person come to mind who could use exactly that this week. Don't plan it all out. Just decide: I'll do it, and I won't mention it. Then rest in the decision for the length of the sit. If you pray, you can offer the work before you do it. The bell holds the time.
Seva. Service done because it's needed, with the self out of the way. Hanuman carrying the mountain. Fifteenth word.
Your line: do something for someone, quietly. One small thing today. No post. No mention. Just a mountain moved, and nobody told. Day fifteen.

16.title: love as a method
16.hook: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water: what the Gita says is enough
16.howItsDone: Bhakti shapes Hindu worship in temples and homes: devotees sing bhajans and kirtan, offer flowers, fruit and water at home shrines and temples, and repeat the names of God, often together and out loud.

segments.voice: Yesterday, seva, and Hanuman with a mountain in his hands. Your line was do something for someone, quietly. If you did it, did some part of you want to tell somebody? Day sixteen.

A leaf. A flower. A piece of fruit. A little water. That list came up on day eight, at the home shrine, and back then the point was how small the gifts are. Today, read the rest of the sentence. In the ninth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that whoever offers him one of these with love, he accepts it, because it was offered with love. The gift isn't what makes it count. The love is. And the Sanskrit word for that love sits right inside the verse. A whole way of walking this path is built on it, a way full of songs, drums, bells and late nights of singing. It's today's word.
screen: `A LEAF, A FLOWER, AGAIN.` → `OFFERED WITH LOVE.` → `THE WORD INSIDE THE VERSE.`

segments.voice: Bhakti. Devotion. Love turned toward God and practiced on purpose, the way you'd practice an instrument. You've spent some of this camp with the head: atman, Brahman, the self and the whole. Bhakti is the heart, and the Gita treats it as a full path of its own. In the Gita's telling, nobody has to master the ideas first. The way in is love. Devotees aim that love at God in different forms, Krishna, Rama, Shiva, the Goddess, and the move is the same. Tradition remembers a woman who showed it. Mirabai was a princess in what is now Rajasthan, and the stories say that from childhood she thought of Krishna as her own. Married into a royal family, she kept singing to him in the temple, in public, with ordinary devotees. Her in-laws, the stories go, were furious. They sent her poison, and it did her no harm. Whatever you make of those details, her songs are still sung. Here's why bhakti is a method and not only a mood. Moods come and go. The lamp gets lit anyway. The song gets sung on the tired night too. Some who practice it say the feeling catches up with the doing, not the other way around. Go back to the leaf: what the verse looks for is the love it's offered with, and love, on this path, is something you keep doing. And that's why this path can be so loud. Bells, drums, a crowd singing the same name over and over. That's bhakti with the volume up.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: offer a leaf. Sit and breathe. Find one small thing within reach. A sip of water, a flower, a breath, even just your open hand. Hold it for a moment. If you pray, you can offer it, with love, to God in whatever form you know. If you don't, offer it to whatever you love most in the world, and let the feeling be as big as it wants to be. Nobody's watching. The bell holds the time.
Bhakti. Devotion. Love you practice, not only love you feel. A leaf, offered whole. Sixteenth word.
Your line: devotion is a verb. Today, do one loving thing on a day you don't feel like it. That's the method, all of it. Day sixteen.

17.title: the courage not to strike
17.hook: the yoga list that starts before any pose: not-harming
17.carry: do no harm — start with your mouth
17.howItsDone: In Hindu life ahimsa shows up in vegetarian kitchens, care for animals and restraint in speech, and yoga teachers present it as the first of the restraints in Patanjali's Yoga Sutras.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti, love practiced like an instrument. Your line was devotion is a verb. Did you do the loving thing on a day you didn't feel like it? Today's word asks for a different kind of strength. Day seventeen.

A message comes in late at night. It's unfair, and it stings, and your thumbs already know the reply. The sharp one. The one that would land. Here's a strange fact about yoga. Before the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali teach anything about posture, they set out a short list of restraints, the ground the rest is built on, and the first word on that list isn't stretch, or breathe. It's not-harming. Which means the first restraint in the text is about those thumbs, right now.
screen: `A MESSAGE. A SHARP REPLY READY.` → `YOGA BEFORE THE POSES.` → `THE FIRST WORD: NOT-HARMING.`

segments.voice: Ahimsa. Himsa is harm, violence. Ahimsa is its opposite: not-harming. And it's easy to hear that as a soft word, a word for people who never stand up for anything. Gandhi, who put this word beside truth at the center of his public life, heard it the other way around. He was not a quiet man. He confronted an empire, and he refused the one weapon everyone expected him to pick up. Ahimsa takes nerve. When something hits a person, the body often wants to hit back, and ahimsa is the half-second where you don't add more harm to a moment that already has some. The Jains, close neighbors on the same soil, hold ahimsa at the heart of their path too. Now look at what Patanjali says comes of it. The Yoga Sutras teach that when someone is truly settled in not-harming, hostility falls away in their presence. Not because they won the argument. Because they stopped feeding it. Some teachers name three places ahimsa lives: in thought, in word, and in deed. Deeds are the obvious ones. Today's line starts with the middle one, words, because that's where the half-second is easiest to miss. The cutting joke. The thing said about someone who isn't in the room. The reply sent at night. One more layer. The vow points inward too. A voice in the head that calls a person worthless is himsa as well. Not-harming includes the one doing the not-harming.
screen: `AHIMSA — NOT-HARMING.` · `NOT SOFT. IT TAKES NERVE.` · `HOSTILITY FALLS AWAY.` · `THOUGHT, WORD, DEED.` · then, large: `START WITH YOUR MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the half-second. Sit and breathe. Bring back the last time you said something sharp, to someone or about someone. Don't punish yourself for it; that would be harm too. Just replay it, slowly, and this time stop at the moment before the words came out. Feel the push to strike. Let it pass through without acting on it. What could have been said instead? Maybe nothing. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Ahimsa. Not-harming, in thought, word and deed. The courage not to strike. Seventeenth word.
Your line: do no harm — start with your mouth. Today, let one sharp sentence go unsaid, and notice what happens to the room. Day seventeen.

screen: `DAY 17 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHY THE WORLD LOOKS SOLID.`

18.title: why the world looks solid
18.hook: a rope on a dark path, and the snake that was never there
18.howItsDone: Hindu teachers explain maya through stories like the rope and the snake, and the schools of Vedanta read it in different ways, some as the appearance of the world over Brahman, others as God's real and wondrous power.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ahimsa, the courage not to strike. Your line was do no harm — start with your mouth. Did a sharp sentence go unsaid? Today we go back to the big ideas for a day. Day eighteen.
screen: `DO NO HARM — START WITH YOUR MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Dusk, on a path, and something is coiled across it. Your heart jumps before your mind has a word for it. Snake. You freeze. Your pulse is real. The fear is real. Then someone brings a lamp, and it's a rope. Just a rope, lying where it always was. Nothing about the rope changed. The snake was never there. And yet for a few seconds it ran your whole body. Teachers in this tradition tell that small story because it holds a very big word. A thing that is not what it seems, and works on you anyway.
screen: `SOMETHING COILED ON THE PATH.` → `THE FEAR IS REAL.` → `A LAMP. A ROPE.`

segments.voice: Maya. It often gets translated as illusion, and that one word causes a lot of confusion. It sounds like the tradition is saying the world is fake. Your kitchen, your friends, your job, none of it real. That isn't what it says. The Svetasvatara Upanishad puts it this way: know that nature is maya, and that the great Lord is the one who works the maya. So maya isn't nothing. It's the power that makes the world appear the way it does, so convincingly that we stop looking past it. Schools of the tradition read this differently, and they've argued about it with great care. Advaita Vedanta, the school of Shankara, says the world we see is an appearance laid over Brahman, the way the snake is laid over the rope. The rope is what's really there. Other schools, like those of Ramanuja and Madhva, hold that the world is fully real, made by God, and that maya names God's wondrous power. Both readings agree on one thing. The surface is not the whole story. And that's where the word walks into an ordinary day. A post makes someone's life look perfect. A comment feels like an attack on all of you. A bad morning looks like a bad life. Each one is a snake on the path, until the lamp comes. Neither reading asks anyone to stop living in the world. Only to stop gripping it as if the surface were everything. Hold it lightly.
screen: `NOT FAKE. NOT THE WHOLE STORY.` · `THE POWER THAT MAKES IT APPEAR.` · `SNAKE ON A ROPE, OR GOD'S POWER?` · `A POST. A COMMENT. A BAD MORNING.` · then, large: `HOLD IT LIGHTLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring the lamp. Sit and breathe. Recall one thing this week that made your heart jump. A message, a look, a number, a picture of someone else's life. Feel the jump again, just a little. Don't push it away. Now look at it again, slowly, as if someone had brought a lamp. What is actually there? Let the tightness loosen as much as it wants to. The bell holds the time.
Maya. The power that makes the world appear, so well that we stop looking past the surface. The snake that turns out to be rope. Eighteenth word.
Your line: hold it lightly. Today, when something makes you jump, take one breath and ask: snake, or rope? Day eighteen.

19.title: the exit door
19.hook: a boy at Death's door turns down every treasure for one question
19.howItsDone: In Hindu thought moksha is named alongside dharma, artha and kama as an aim of life, and seekers pursue it through knowledge, devotion, selfless action and meditation, with each school describing liberation in its own way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, maya, and the snake that was a rope. Your line was hold it lightly. Did you catch a snake on the path? Today, the word for where this whole path is headed. Day nineteen.

A boy named Nachiketa is sitting at the door of Death's house. In the Katha Upanishad, his father, in a burst of temper, has said: I give you to Death. So the boy goes. Yama, the lord of death, is away, and Nachiketa waits on the doorstep without food for three nights. When Yama comes home, he's embarrassed to have kept a guest waiting, and he offers the boy three wishes. The first two are easy. The third is a question: what happens to a person after death? Yama tries to talk him out of it. Ask for something else, he says. Ask for long life, sons and grandsons, cattle, gold, a kingdom. Nachiketa says no.
screen: `A BOY AT DEATH'S DOOR.` → `THREE WISHES.` → `TAKE THE GOLD INSTEAD.` → `NO.`

segments.voice: Nachiketa's answer is the heart of today's word. He tells Death that all those treasures wear out, that wealth will never satisfy a person, that even a long life is short. Keep your horses, he says. I want to know. And Yama, impressed, begins to teach him. That turn, from the list of things to the thing under the list, points straight at today's word. Moksha means release. Liberation. Freedom. The tradition speaks of the soul moving through birth after birth, bound by its own actions and desires, and moksha is the knot finally coming untied. Hindu thought names several aims of a good life: dharma, doing what's yours to do; artha, making a living; kama, love and pleasure. None of those are bad. Moksha sits beyond them, as the freedom the others point toward. What that freedom is, the schools describe differently. Advaita Vedanta says it's waking up to what day ten and day eleven already hinted: that atman, the self, is Brahman, and always was. Devotional schools, such as those centered on Krishna, describe it as living forever in the loving presence of God, never dissolved, never alone. Some schools teach that a person can be free before death, liberated while still living. Notice the shape of Nachiketa's choice. He doesn't hate gold. He just won't trade the real question for it. That's the word in an ordinary day too: the moment you see that the next thing on the list was never going to be enough.
screen: `KEEP YOUR HORSES. I WANT TO KNOW.` · `MOKSHA — RELEASE. THE KNOT UNTIED.` · `BEYOND DUTY, WEALTH AND PLEASURE.` · `ATMAN IS BRAHMAN, OR LOVE WITH GOD.` · then, large: `FREEDOM IS THE POINT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set one thing down. Sit and breathe. Notice one thing you want right now. A message back, a better week, a number on a screen. Let the wanting be there. Now, just for the length of this sit, set it down beside you. Not forever. Just: for now, I don't need it. Breathe, and notice what's left when the wanting rests. If you pray, you can hold that space open to God. The bell holds the time.
Moksha. Release. Liberation. The knot untied, the freedom the other aims of life point toward. Nineteenth word.
Your line: freedom is the point. Once today, when you catch yourself chasing the next thing, set it down for one breath, the way Nachiketa set down the gold. Day nineteen.

20.title: good company
20.hook: an old chain of verses that starts with who you sit with and ends in freedom
20.howItsDone: Hindus gather for satsang in homes, temples and ashrams to sing bhajans, hear a teacher, read scripture together and sit in silence, and some families hold one on special days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, moksha, and a boy who told Death to keep his gold. Your line was freedom is the point. Did you set something down, even for a breath? One more word before the camp ends. Day twenty.

Yesterday's word was the top of the mountain: freedom. Fair question, then. Where do you start? There's an old Sanskrit song called Bhaja Govindam, traditionally credited to the teacher Shankara, and one of its verses answers that question like a row of dominoes. Each step knocks over the next, all the way up to freedom. You'd expect the first domino to be something hard. Years of study. Fasting. A cave in the mountains. It isn't. The very first domino is who you spend your time with.
screen: `WHERE DO YOU START?` → `A ROW OF DOMINOES.` → `THE FIRST ONE: YOUR COMPANY.`

segments.voice: Satsang. Sat means true, real, good. Sang means company, being together. Satsang is good company, the company of what's true and of people turned toward it. Here's the chain from Bhaja Govindam, in plain words. From good company comes letting go. From letting go comes freedom from delusion. From freedom from delusion comes a mind that stays steady. And from a steady mind comes freedom while you're still alive. Look at what's in that chain. Delusion: think of the snake on the rope from day eighteen. Freedom is moksha from yesterday. And the thing that starts it all isn't a technique. It's a room. In Hindu life, a satsang is often an actual gathering. People meet in a home or a temple hall to sing, to hear a teacher, to read a text together, to sit in silence side by side. Nobody has to be advanced. You come, you sit, you listen. The idea underneath the verse is simple and a little uncomfortable: company shapes a person. A friend's worries can become your worries; a grandmother's patience can become your patience. The verse doesn't say go find perfect people. It puts company first in the chain, and leaves the question with you: what is your company doing to you, and how much time do you spend near what's true? That first domino has a name and a face.
screen: `SAT — TRUE. SANG — COMPANY.` · `GOOD COMPANY, THEN LETTING GO, THEN FREEDOM.` · `A ROOM, NOT A TECHNIQUE.` · `WE TAKE THE SHAPE OF OUR COMPANY.` · then, large: `GOOD COMPANY CHANGES YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit in company. Sit and breathe. Bring to mind one person whose presence makes you steadier. A friend, a grandparent, a teacher, someone in a story. Let their face come. Notice what happens to your breathing near them. Then widen it, to anyone, anywhere, who stops today to pray or to sit still. Let yourself be one of them. If you pray, you can hold them all before God. The bell holds the time.
Satsang. Good company. The company of what's true, and the first domino on the way to freedom. Twentieth word.
Your line: good company changes you. Today, spend ten unhurried minutes with one person who steadies you. In person, if you can. Day twenty.

21.title: the mountain ahead
21.hook: back to the battlefield: a warrior drops his bow, and the conversation begins
21.carry: you have the right to act. Not to the fruit
21.howItsDone: Hindus read and recite the Bhagavad Gita at home, in temples and in study groups, and some memorize its verses; its teaching on action without attachment to results is quoted in daily life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, satsang. Your line was good company changes you. Now, the whole camp, quickly: namaste, om, dharma, shanti, pranam, Ganesha, mantra, puja, karma, atman, Brahman, guru, japa, arti, seva, bhakti, ahimsa, maya, moksha, satsang. Twenty words. Today makes twenty-one. Day twenty-one.

segments.voice: Go back to day three. A battlefield, two armies drawn up, conch shells blowing. Arjuna, a great archer, asks his charioteer to drive him out between the lines so he can see who he's about to fight. He looks across and sees teachers, uncles, cousins, friends. His mouth goes dry. His bow slips from his hand. And he sits down in the chariot and says he will not fight. We left him there, with his driver, Krishna, beside him. Today we find out what happens next. Because the whole conversation that follows has a name, and it's the last word of this camp.
screen: `BACK TO THE BATTLEFIELD.` → `HIS BOW SLIPS.` → `WHAT DOES THE DRIVER SAY?`

segments.voice: The Bhagavad Gita. The Song of the Lord. It sits inside the great epic, the Mahabharata, and it's a conversation between two people in a chariot. On day three you heard that the driver is Krishna, and a great deal more than a driver. Krishna does more than give orders. He teaches. He talks about the self that cannot be killed, which you met as atman. He talks about acting without grabbing, about loving God, about seeing clearly. Look back at this week and you'll hear echoes. Action with the self out of the way, the way seva works. Love as a path of its own, bhakti. The Gita holds these paths side by side. Then the line this camp saved for last. In the second chapter Krishna says, in plain words: your right is to the action alone, never to its fruits. Don't let the fruit be your reason for acting. And the verse keeps going: don't let that become a reason to do nothing, either. It isn't a way out of the fight. It's a way to stand up and act without being owned by the result. And near the end of the Gita comes a surprise. After everything, Krishna tells Arjuna to think it over fully, and then do as he chooses. He hands the choice back. In the fourth camp you'll read this text itself, line by line. For now you get the door, and the sentence that opens it.
screen: `THE SONG OF THE LORD, IN A CHARIOT.` · `THE WHOLE CAMP IS IN THERE.` · `NOT A WAY OUT. A WAY TO STAND UP.` · `THINK IT OVER. THEN CHOOSE.` · then, large: `YOU HAVE THE RIGHT TO ACT. NOT TO THE FRUIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick up the bow. Sit and breathe. Press your palms together at your chest, the way you did on day one. Bring to mind one thing that's yours to do this week, the thing you've been sitting down in the chariot about. Picture doing it, fully. Then open your hand, and let go of how it turns out. The action is yours. The fruit isn't. If you pray, you can offer the result to God. The bell holds the time.
The Gita. The Song of the Lord, a conversation in a chariot that gets a warrior back on his feet. Twenty-first word, and the door to the mountain.
screen: `THE GITA — your 21st word` → the strand complete → `CAMP 1. FIRST WORDS. DONE.`

segments.voice: Your line: you have the right to act. Not to the fruit. Do one thing today that's yours to do, and let the result go. Tomorrow the stories begin, with a goddess, a bath, and a boy made of earth. Day twenty-one.
